Modern.brandDescription: Repower Works converts diesel delivery vans and box trucks into electric vehicles on a serialized production line, not a project bench. Every conversion gets a remanufactured-vehicle serial number, a dyno sheet, and a warranty written like new-equipment paper. The pattern is simple: retrofit treated as remanufacturing, with the discipline of a factory and none of the romance of a workshop. Fleets keep the chassis they already own and get back a truck that reports like a new one.
Modern.scope: Three donor platforms only: step vans, Class 4 box trucks, and cargo vans, each with a locked bill of materials. Brand covers the conversion line, the fleet-facing telemetry portal, and the certified pre-owned repower program. No consumer conversions, no one-offs.

Modern.industrySummary: Commercial EV retrofit sharpened into a real market in 2025-26 as the US commercial clean vehicle credit sunset in late 2025 and pushed fleets toward cheaper electrification paths than new trucks. First-generation conversion players consolidated — SEA Electric was absorbed by Exro, Lightning eMotors collapsed — leaving demand from parcel and food-distribution fleets underserved. A mid-life repower now runs roughly half the cost of a comparable new electric truck while reusing a chassis the fleet has already depreciated. Buyers in 2026 ask two questions: is it certified, and who backs the warranty — which is exactly where hobby-grade converters fail.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Evolectric (evolectric.com) converts commercial fleets with a kit-and-partner model; Bedeo (bedeo.tech) retrofits vans in the UK with in-wheel motors and range-extender options; Harbinger (harbingermotors.com) sells new purpose-built medium-duty EV chassis rather than conversions. None of the three runs a serialized remanufacturing line with new-equipment warranty paper — that is the open lane.
Modern.positioningStatement: The conversion house that builds retrofits to remanufacturing standard — serialized, warrantied, and boring on purpose.
Modern.positioningRationale: Fleet managers do not buy conversions; they buy the absence of risk. By borrowing the language and paperwork of remanufacturing — an industry fleets already trust for engines and transmissions — Repower Works reframes retrofit from experiment to established practice. Everyone else in the segment still sounds like a garage.

They answer to a CFO on total cost of ownership and to a board on emissions targets. They have been burned by at least one EV pilot and now demand warranty terms before demo rides. Age and lifestyle are irrelevant; spreadsheet literacy is total.

Repower Works was incorporated the month the last one shipped, and the survey format became the production traveler that follows every truck down the line today.

Modern.brandDescription: Datum Calibration is an ADAS calibration network that publishes its accuracy and re-fault data the way a lab publishes results. Every windshield camera, radar, and lidar sensor calibrated in a Datum Calibration bay gets a signed certificate with target distances, tolerances achieved, and a public audit trail insurers can query. One idea drives everything: calibration is metrology, and metrology without published numbers is theater.
Modern.scope: Fixed calibration centers plus dispatch-grade mobile rigs serving collision shops, glass installers, and fleets. The brand covers the certificate system, the technician certification ladder, and the insurer-facing audit API. No general repair, no glass installation.
Modern.brandNameRationale: A datum is the machinist's and surveyor's term for the fixed reference point from which every other measurement is taken — the exact job an ADAS target board performs. It signals precision culture to trade audiences without explanation.
Modern.industrySummary: By 2025 more than nine in ten new US vehicles carry ADAS features that require recalibration after windshield replacement, suspension work, or collision repair, and the calibration services market is compounding at double-digit rates through 2026. Insurers have begun auditing calibration invoices after a wave of documentation-free charges, and OEM position statements now specify calibration events in granular detail. The trade's dirty secret is variance: two shops can both claim a completed calibration with no comparable evidence. A network that treats each event as an auditable measurement, with data insurers can verify, sells trust in a market currently priced on assertion.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Protech Automotive Solutions (protechas.com) runs a national mobile ADAS calibration fleet serving collision shops; Car ADAS Solutions (caradas.com) licenses and equips dedicated calibration centers; AirPro Diagnostics (airprodiagnostics.com) provides remote diagnostics and calibration support tools. All three sell capability; none publishes accuracy or re-fault data publicly — Datum competes on audited proof.
Modern.positioningStatement: The only calibration network that shows its work — every sensor, every tolerance, on the record.
Modern.positioningRationale: When insurers start auditing a category, the winner is whoever industrializes proof first. Publishing accuracy data is painful, which is precisely why it is defensible: competitors with variance cannot follow.

One flat monthly price, swap when life changes, cancel like a gym you actually liked. Loaner takes the single beloved ritual in automotive retail and stretches it into an ownership model.

Modern.industrySummary: Car subscription shook out hard into 2025: Onto collapsed in the UK, Autonomy retreated in the US, and the survivors — notably FINN, which scaled past 25,000 vehicles — proved the model works on used and mainstream cars with disciplined unit economics rather than aspirational EV fleets. Elevated new-car prices and insurance premiums through 2025-26 keep pushing urban professionals toward bundled monthly mobility over 72-month loans. The unresolved problem is emotional, not financial: subscriptions still feel like rental-counter bureaucracy. The winner sells the feeling of the effortless handover, not the spreadsheet.

Modern.positioningRationale: Category competitors differentiate on fleet mix and pricing, which customers cannot feel. Loaner differentiates on a named, familiar ritual — the loaner handover — which every customer has experienced and can instantly imagine subscribing to. Borrowed familiarity beats explained innovation.

Modern.brandDescription: Assay Auto Labs is an independent battery-health certification house for used electric vehicles. Each pack is tested against a published protocol and stamped with a state-of-health grade — a hallmark for the battery age, backed by a searchable registry that follows the VIN for life. Assay Auto Labs takes no commission on any sale it grades, because an assayer who profits from the metal is no assayer at all. The grade appears on the windshield, in the listing, and in the lender's file, identically.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Assaying is the seven-century-old practice of independently testing precious metal before it may be stamped — the London assay offices have hallmarked silver since 1327, and the word hallmark itself comes from Goldsmiths' Hall. Applying the assay office model to battery packs imports an institution built precisely for high-value goods whose quality is invisible to the buyer.
Modern.industrySummary: The used-EV wave broke in 2025-26 as the lease boom of 2022-23 returned hundreds of thousands of off-lease EVs to a market with no trusted way to price their batteries, while steep depreciation made battery uncertainty the single largest discount factor on used EV values. Diagnostic players like Recurrent and Aviloo proved demand for health reports, and the EU's battery passport requirement arriving in early 2027 is pushing the whole industry toward standardized disclosure. What remains missing is an independent, non-transactional certifier whose grade lenders and insurers will underwrite against. Whoever becomes the assay office for packs sets the market's reference price.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Recurrent (recurrentauto.com) generates battery range reports for US used-EV shoppers and dealers from telematics data; Aviloo (aviloo.com) sells plug-in battery test boxes and certificates across Europe; ClearWatt (clearwatt.co.uk) provides independent EV health checks for UK consumers and remarketers. All three sell reports; none operates a no-commission registry graded to a published protocol that lenders underwrite against — the assay-office position is open.
Modern.positioningStatement: The independent assay office for EV batteries — tested to a published standard, stamped for life, never party to the sale.
Modern.positioningRationale: Trust infrastructure wins by conspicuous disinterest: the certifier must have nothing to gain from the transaction. By adopting the assay office's ancient governance — published protocol, permanent registry, zero commission — Assay Auto Labs positions itself as the reference authority rather than another vendor of reports.

The chain adopts together or not at all, so the brand speaks institution-first.

Luxury.brandDescription: Ampère & Cie is a classic-EV restomod house that works the way fine printmakers do: one marque chosen per year, an edition of twelve conversions, each numbered in a sealed ledger and never repeated. A 1972 Citroën DS year is followed by a Jaguar year, then the plate is retired — the tooling archived, the edition closed. Ampère & Cie treats electrification not as modernization but as conservation: the coachwork untouched, the drivetrain reversible, the silence considered part of the restoration. Commissions open each January and close when the ledger does.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: André-Marie Ampère is the Lyon-born physicist whose name is stamped on every fuse, charger, and current rating in the electric world — the most literal possible patron for electrified classics. The suffix & Cie is the traditional French trading-house form, placing the atelier in the lineage of nineteenth-century maisons rather than twenty-first-century startups.
Luxury.industrySummary: The classic-EV restomod trade hardened into a genuine luxury category through 2025-26, with UK houses like Lunaz and Everrati commanding £250,000-plus commissions and waiting lists measured in quarters. Buyer sophistication rose with the market: collectors now demand reversible conversions that preserve matching-numbers value, and originality debates dominate concours committees. Supply of skilled conversion labor, not demand, is the binding constraint, which rewards ateliers that constrain output deliberately. The unclaimed position is editioning — no house has yet applied the print-room logic of closed, numbered editions to conversion.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Lunaz (lunaz.design) electrifies Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Range Rover classics from Silverstone; Everrati (everrati.com) converts Porsche 911s, GT40s, and Land Rovers with OEM-grade engineering; Electrogenic (electrogenic.co.uk) offers drop-in EV kits and bespoke conversions for British and French classics. All three convert continuously across marques on demand; none closes editions — Ampère & Cie's scarcity is structural, not rhetorical.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The restomod atelier that works in closed editions — one marque a year, twelve cars, then never again.
Luxury.positioningRationale: Luxury value accrues to verifiable scarcity, and continuous-commission houses cannot offer it. The sealed ledger converts a service business into an editioned-object business, letting each year's cars appreciate as a set and giving collectors a reason to buy the edition rather than merely a conversion.

Psychologically they are completists: the appeal is not owning an electric DS but owning number seven of the only twelve that will ever exist. They commission by referral, visit the atelier twice during the build, and care as much about the ledger entry as the car.

She numbered her working ledger out of workshop habit — page one, car one — and when a collector offered to buy the car, he asked instead what number he could commission. The question became the company: if the ledger is the object of desire, close it at twelve and start a new marque each year. Ampère & Cie has opened its ledger every January since, and no edition has taken longer than a fortnight to fill.

Luxury.brandDescription: The Motor Livery is a collector-car stewardship house that borrowed its model from the racehorse world: cars are not stored, they are boarded. Each vehicle has a named keeper, an exercise schedule, a bound logbook of every start, drive, and fluid change, and a standing appointment with the seasons — summer tyres, winter fogging, spring recommissioning. The Motor Livery answers the question wealthy owners actually have, which is not where the car sleeps but who loves it on the days they cannot. Membership is by the car, not the square foot.
Luxury.scope: Climate-controlled boarding with keeper-led exercise programs, transport concierge, pre-event preparation, and logbook stewardship across two metropolitan houses. The brand covers boarding, exercise, and documentation services. No sales brokerage, no restoration work beyond recommissioning.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: A livery stable is the centuries-old institution where owners boarded horses under professional care — livery meaning kept, fed, and exercised at another's establishment. Transposing livery to motorcars names the exact service gap between dead storage and ownership, with an aristocratic echo the clientele hears immediately.
Luxury.industrySummary: Collector-car storage demand outran supply through 2025-26 as urban collectors accumulated more vehicles than home garages hold, with premium facilities like Windrush in London and Hagerty's expanding Garage + Social network proving members will pay hotel rates for automotive real estate. The market's growth edge shifted from square footage to service: exercised cars hold value dramatically better than parked ones, and insurers increasingly price condition monitoring. Auction results in 2025 punished unexercised, long-stored examples with recommissioning discounts. Storage is a commodity; stewardship — documented, scheduled, personal — is the open luxury position.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Windrush Car Storage (windrushcarstorage.co.uk) offers white-glove long-term storage in London and the Cotswolds; Hagerty Garage + Social (garageandsocial.com) combines premium storage with clubhouse membership across North America; Autovault (autovault.co.uk) provides secure bespoke vehicle storage in the UK. All three sell space and security first; none structures the offer around keeper-led exercise and logbook stewardship — the livery model itself.

Luxury.positioningRationale: The category anchors price to floor space, which caps margin and commoditizes the offer. Anchoring to the racehorse-livery model reprices the service around care per animal — per car — and creates an emotional contract (someone loves it while you are away) no warehouse can match.

Luxury.manifesto: A car is not a painting. It was built to be warm, to circulate its fluids, to feel weight transfer through a corner — and it dies, slowly and expensively, standing still. We believe boarding a car means what boarding a horse has always meant: a keeper who knows its temperament, a schedule kept whether the owner visits or not, and a book in which nothing is omitted. We start them in the dark of winter. We drive them gently on Tuesday mornings. We write it all down. Your car should be exercised, not embalmed.

Luxury.brandDescription: The Salon Practice is a consultancy that rebuilds luxury dealership experience on a single conviction: the car showroom was born as a salon — the 1898 Paris Salon de l'Automobile, where machines were presented like works in an exhibition — and a century of sales-floor thinking has buried it. The Salon Practice re-stages luxury retail spaces around hospitality ritual: staff hired from hotels and galleries rather than car lots, no desks, no F&I corridor, commissions restructured around relationship tenure. Engagements run eighteen months and end with the client's showroom operating, measurably, like a great house rather than a point of sale.
Luxury.scope: Advisory and implementation for luxury and premium-EV retailers: spatial reprogramming, hospitality hiring and training systems, compensation redesign, and post-launch measurement. Typically one flagship per client, then a rollout playbook. No mass-market dealer work, no software licensing.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: The Salon de l'Automobile of 1898 in the Grand Palais gardens was the world's first true motor show — cars staged as cultural objects among promenading guests, decades before the fluorescent sales floor existed. Practice is borrowed from architecture and medicine: a body of working method, applied case by case.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury automotive retail entered 2025-26 squeezed from both sides: direct-sales EV entrants reset customer expectations for transparent, pressure-free purchase, while several European agency-model experiments retreated and handed experience back to retailers unsure what to do with it. US franchise dealers, flush from the margin years but facing normalizing inventories, are investing in CX differentiation as pricing converges. Meanwhile luxury consumers benchmarked against Aman service and Apple retail rate the traditional F&I gauntlet as the worst purchase experience in their lives. The consultancies serving dealers still optimize funnels; nobody owns the hospitality-conversion position.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: MSX International (msxi.com) delivers dealer performance and retail-transformation programs for OEM networks; Urban Science (urbanscience.com) advises on dealer network strategy with data science; J.D. Power (jdpower.com) benchmarks and consults on customer experience across automotive retail. All three approach experience through metrics and network math; none rebuilds the showroom on hospitality staffing and salon ritual — The Salon Practice's entire method.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The consultancy that turns luxury showrooms back into salons — hospitality-run rooms where cars are presented, not sold.
Luxury.positioningRationale: Every incumbent advisor optimizes the existing sales model; The Salon Practice replaces its DNA, hiring from a different industry entirely. The 1898 anchor gives the method a legitimacy no framework deck can match: this is restoration of the showroom's original form, not innovation upon it.

The trigger moment is competitive: a direct-sales gallery opening across the road, or a brand survey score they cannot present to the principal's family board.

Luxury.manifesto: In 1898 they showed automobiles in the gardens of the Grand Palais, and people came dressed for it. Somewhere between then and now, the salon became a floor, the guest became an up, and the most expensive purchase of a family's year came to smell of toner and desperation. We are not here to digitize that. We are here to end it. Hire the maître d', not the closer. Burn the desks. Pour something good. Luxury.tagline: Twelve members. One season. A racing licence.
Luxury.brandDescription: The Slipstream Club is a motorsport academy structured as a private members' club: an annual cohort of twelve, a clubhouse at the circuit, and a single shared objective — from road driver to holder of a national racing licence in one season. Members progress together through simulator blocks, car-control school, test days, and their first three sanctioned races, with coaching staffed at one-to-two and a club dinner after every round. The Slipstream Club sells what money alone cannot arrange: a structured, social, genuinely earned entry into racing. When the season ends, members keep the licence, the lap data, and each other.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: The slipstream is racing's most social phenomenon — the pocket of moving air behind a faster car that tows the driver behind, immortalized in the four-abreast slipstreaming battles of 1960s Monza. It is the perfect name for an academy whose method is cohort tow: nobody gets to race pace alone.
Luxury.industrySummary: Motorsport participation among affluent adults kept climbing through 2025-26 on the momentum of Drive to Survive's audiences, F1's US expansion, and simulator culture that converts spectators into aspirants; racing schools like Radford and Skip Barber report record enrollment and waiting lists for advanced programs. Yet the path from track-day dabbling to an actual racing licence remains fragmented across schools, clubs, and test days that share no curriculum. Arrive-and-drive series lowered the machinery barrier while leaving the social and procedural barriers intact. A cohort-based, licence-guaranteed season — priced like a club membership rather than a course — is the structural gap.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Skip Barber Racing School (skipbarber.com) runs racing schools and licensing programs at US circuits; Radford Racing School (radfordracing.com) operates full-immersion performance and racing curricula in Arizona; Porsche Track Experience (porsche.com) delivers brand-led driver development up to racing-licence level. All three sell courses to individuals on calendar dates; none builds a fixed cohort with club structure and a season-long arc — the Slipstream model.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The members' club where the membership is a racing season — and the graduation gift is a licence.
Luxury.positioningRationale: Affluent aspirants do not lack money or courses; they lack structure, cohort, and permission. Framing the academy as a club with a class year imports the social mechanics of business schools and expedition companies — shared ordeal, lifetime bond — which no pay-per-day racing school can replicate.

Psychographically they are earned-credential people; unstructured indulgence bores them and examined progress thrills them. Half arrive from sim racing with hundreds of virtual hours and zero real grid starts.

Luxury.story: The club began when a retired touring-car coach agreed to take a hedge-fund founder from zero to a national licence in a single season — on the condition that he bring five friends, because, as the coach put it, nobody learns race craft alone; you learn it in the tow. The six trained as a unit, dined as a unit after every test day, and five of the six passed their licence tests on the first attempt — a rate the coach had never seen teaching individuals. Word moved through two dinner parties and a paddock; the second cohort filled in nine days. The founders capped it at twelve, hired a clubhouse steward before a marketing manager, and The Slipstream Club has run one season, one cohort, ever since.

Luxury.tagline: Fitted out for the far interior.
Luxury.brandDescription: Beaufort Overland builds expedition vehicle interiors to yacht standard — naval joinery, marine electrical architecture, and water systems engineered by people who learned their trade fitting out ocean-going sailboats. Each commission is a single 4x4 chassis transformed over roughly nine months into a vehicle capable of six weeks beyond infrastructure, then proven on a documented thousand-mile shakedown the company calls the sea trial. Beaufort Overland exists for owners who noticed that the RV industry builds furniture and the yacht industry builds systems, and who intend to cross Namibia with the second kind.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: Sir Francis Beaufort was the Royal Navy hydrographer whose wind scale still governs every mariner's weather judgment — a name synonymous with measured preparation for hostile environments. Borrowing it for overland expedition builds signals the transfer of maritime seriousness to land travel.
Luxury.industrySummary: The expedition vehicle market matured past its pandemic surge into a bifurcated 2025-26: casual vanlife demand cooled while the serious end — six-figure global-travel trucks — kept multi-quarter waitlists at builders like EarthRoamer and Krug. Buyers at this tier now shop internationally, compare water and power systems like yacht surveyors, and increasingly plan multi-year circumnavigations enabled by remote work and early retirement. Quality variance remains the category scandal: cabinet-grade builds fail in corrugation conditions that marine-grade systems shrug off. The vocabulary of naval architecture — displacement, systems redundancy, sea trials — is sitting unused in a category that needs it.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: EarthRoamer (earthroamer.com) builds luxury expedition vehicles on Ford chassis in Colorado; Krug Expedition (krugxp.com) constructs global-travel trucks on MAN and Steyr platforms in Austria; Loki Basecamp (lokibasecamp.com) produces premium truck-camper modules in Canada. All three build from an RV or camper lineage; none stakes its method on yacht fit-out standards and documented sea trials — Beaufort's entire construction.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Expedition vehicles built like ocean-going yachts — joinery, systems, and sea trials included.
Luxury.positioningRationale: At this price tier, buyers fear system failure a thousand miles from help more than they desire any feature; marine standards are the strongest available proxy for survivable engineering. The yacht anchor also imports a commissioning culture — surveys, trials, handover documentation — that justifies the price and the wait.

targetAudience.primary: Couples in their late forties to mid-sixties at the threshold of a long-planned chapter: the two-year Pan-American drive, the Africa crossing, the retirement spent between continents. Many are sailors or former sailors — people who already trust marine systems with their lives and are fluent in redundancy, wattage, and water budgets. They commission eighteen months ahead, interview builders like they once surveyed yachts, and read handover manuals for pleasure.

Minimal.brandDescription: CONTACT PATCH is a tire subscription with a one-page catalog: one all-season tire model engineered in four sizes, one flat monthly price, fitted and rotated at your kerb. No brand tiers, no seasonal upsell, no waiting room with a television bolted to the wall. CONTACT PATCH covers wear, punctures, rotation, and replacement for as long as you subscribe, because the company's only product is the part of your car that touches the road.
Minimal.scope: Consumer subscription covering supply, mobile fitting, rotation, puncture repair, and end-of-life replacement for passenger cars in launch metros. One tire model, four sizes, one price. No performance tires, no commercial fleets at launch.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: The contact patch is the genuine tire-engineering term for the postcard-sized area where each tire actually meets the road — the only four points a car touches the world. Naming the company for it reduces the entire category to its irreducible fact.
Minimal.industrySummary: Tire economics turned against the consumer through 2025-26: replacement tire prices climbed roughly a fifth above pre-2021 levels, EVs wear tires meaningfully faster due to weight and torque, and the average buyer confronts a wall of hundreds of near-identical SKUs priced opaquely. Tires-as-a-service is established in commercial fleets — Michelin has sold by the kilometer for years — but consumer subscription remains unbuilt beyond financing plans dressed as subscriptions. Mobile fitting, proven by companies like Zohr, removed the last logistical excuse. The open play is radical simplification: one good tire, flat pricing, service included.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Blackcircles (blackcircles.com) retails tires online with garage fitting across the UK; Zohr (zohr.com) delivers mobile tire installation at homes and offices in US metros; SimpleTire (simpletire.com) runs a large online tire marketplace with installer partnerships. All three sell transactions across vast SKU catalogs; none offers a single-model flat-rate subscription with service included — CONTACT PATCH's whole premise.
Minimal.positioningStatement: The tire company with one tire — subscribed, fitted at your kerb, never thought about again.
Minimal.positioningRationale: Tire buying is a low-knowledge, high-anxiety purchase where choice is the pain, not the value. Collapsing the catalog to one engineered-well model converts an adversarial decision into a utility, and the subscription aligns the company with longevity rather than replacement volume.

The vans carry every part for the nine jobs, the prices have not got smaller type underneath, and the mechanic who quotes the work does the work — in your driveway, while you get on with your day.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: Spanner is the British trade word for the wrench — the tool that stands for the whole craft in every workshop idiom from throwing one in the works to being spanner-handy. It is a mechanic's word chosen over a marketer's word, which is the brand in miniature.
Minimal.industrySummary: Mobile mechanics moved from fringe to mainstream through 2025-26 as US shop labor rates pushed past 150-250 dollars an hour, the technician shortage ran tens of thousands of positions deep, and an aging car parc — average vehicle age near thirteen years — generated more of exactly the routine work that fits in a driveway. Consolidation followed: AutoNation absorbed RepairSmith into a national mobile arm while independents multiplied on marketplace platforms of uneven quality. Consumer distrust of open-ended quotes remains the category's defining friction. A fixed, short, flat-priced menu is the clearest possible answer, and no one has committed to it.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Wrench (wrench.com) dispatches mobile mechanics across US metros via app booking; YourMechanic (yourmechanic.com) operates a mobile repair marketplace with quoted services; AutoNation Mobile Service (autonationmobileservice.com) runs dealer-backed mobile repair vans nationally. All three quote from sprawling service catalogs; none constrains itself to a short flat-priced menu — SPANNER wins on the honesty of its limits.
Minimal.positioningStatement: The mobile mechanic that does nine jobs perfectly and tells you the truth about the tenth.

Three years on, the fleet is forty vans and the prices are still on the doors, now in better paint.

Minimal.brandDescription: Bothy makes flat-pack camper interiors that turn any empty van into an overnight shelter in an afternoon — and back into a work van in an hour. One birch-ply system: bed platform, galley block, storage spine, sized to the three most common vans and assembled with a single included tool. Bothy is deliberately not a conversion company; it is furniture for vans, built on the belief that most people need forty good nights a year, not a rolling apartment. Buy it once, move it between vans, hand it down.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: A bothy is the Scottish mountain tradition's free stone shelter — unlocked, unstaffed, spartan, and beloved — maintained for any walker who needs a roof for the night. It is the exact philosophy of this product: adequate shelter, zero ceremony, held in common affection.
Minimal.industrySummary: Vanlife's speculative froth burned off through 2024-25, leaving a durable core market of weekenders who balked at 50,000-to-200,000-dollar professional conversions and pandemic-era waitlists. Kit and modular makers — Wayfarer, Adventure Wagon, Happier Camper — proved demand for install-it-yourself interiors at a tenth of conversion cost, while removability emerged as the killer feature for insurance, resale, and lease compliance. Van prices stayed high into 2026, strengthening the case for furniture that outlives any single vehicle. The unclaimed ground is radical simplicity: one system, no options wall, priced like good furniture rather than cheap construction.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Wayfarer Vans (wayfarervans.com) sells simple bolt-in van conversion kits installed in hours; Adventure Wagon (adventurewagon.com) offers modular interior kits with rail systems for Sprinters and Transits; Happier Camper (happiercamper.com) makes the Adaptiv modular fiberglass interior system. All three sell configurable component ecosystems; Bothy sells one considered system with no configurator — the anti-options position.
Minimal.positioningStatement: The one-afternoon camper interior: one kit, one tool, any empty van.
Minimal.positioningRationale: Kit buyers are fleeing complexity, yet every kit brand rebuilds it as a configurator. A single perfected system honors the actual job — forty nights a year of dry sleep and hot coffee — and the bothy ethos gives the austerity a warmth no spec sheet can.

Many already own the van; the empty cargo space behind the seats is a standing reproach.

Minimal.story: The founders, two Scottish product designers, spent a decade of weekends walking between Highland bothies and grew fascinated by how much comfort a stone room with a sleeping platform could hold. Minimal.brandDescription: POOL CAR puts one shared car in the garage of an apartment building, booked by residents the way they book the laundry room. No membership tiers, no surge pricing, no fleet app empire — a clean EV downstairs, a flat hourly rate on the building's own board, keys via a fob that already opens the gym. POOL CAR sells to developers and building managers as an amenity that replaces parking spaces, and to residents it barely sells at all; it is simply there, like the elevator.
Minimal.scope: Amenity car-share for residential buildings: vehicle, insurance, charging, cleaning, and booking system bundled per building on multi-year agreements with developers and HOAs. One to three cars per property. No public floating fleets, no airport service.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: Pool car is the unglamorous fleet-management term for a shared vehicle held in common — the car that belongs to everyone at the office and no one in particular. Applied to a residential building it names the model with zero explanation required, in the same deadpan register as calling the laundry room the laundry room.
Minimal.industrySummary: The economics of building-based car share inverted through 2024-26 as dozens of North American cities eliminated or slashed parking minimums, letting developers trade underground stalls costing 50,000-plus dollars each for shared-mobility amenities that satisfy planners and tenants alike. Amenity carshare operators like Envoy proved the B2B2C model — the building pays, residents ride — while urban car ownership costs pushed past 12,000 dollars a year and made the second household car increasingly indefensible. Insurance and utilization remain the operator's hard problems, favoring dense, closed user groups over public fleets. The category's residual weakness is overcomplication: apps, tiers, and pricing games where a laundry-room booking would do.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Envoy (envoythere.com) provides amenity EV car-share to apartment and office properties across the US; Zipcar (zipcar.com) operates public station-based car share including some residential placements; Kinto (kinto-mobility.com) runs Toyota-backed shared mobility programs in multiple markets. Envoy leads the amenity niche with a broad fleet menu and app-first experience; POOL CAR differentiates on laundry-room simplicity — one car type, flat rate, building-native booking.
Minimal.positioningStatement: One good car per building, booked like the laundry room.
Minimal.positioningRationale: Amenity car share fails on friction, not demand: every added tier and pricing rule suppresses casual bookings that drive utilization. Radical domestic simplicity — flat rate, familiar booking, the fob you already carry — makes the car feel like infrastructure, which is the level at which sharing actually sticks.

Minimal.tagline: The dent leaves. The paint stays.
Minimal.brandDescription: DENT does paintless dent repair and nothing else: no paint, no filler, no bodyshop, no insurance theater. A technician comes to the car, works the metal back from behind with rods and patience, and the factory finish never knows it happened. DENT is built on the belief that the most honest repair is the one that removes itself — door dings, hail strikes, and parking dents erased in under an hour, priced by the dent, guaranteed by photograph.
Minimal.brandNameRationale: The name is the defect itself, stated flat — in the tradition of trades that call the job by its problem, the way roofers talk about the leak and glaziers about the crack. One syllable of damage, and the company exists to delete it.
Minimal.industrySummary: Paintless dent repair boomed through 2024-26 on the back of record hail seasons — US hail claims set new highs with multiple multi-billion-dollar storm events — and on insurers' growing preference for PDR, which costs a fraction of conventional bodywork and preserves factory paint and resale value. Meanwhile average collision repair costs climbed with sensor-laden panels, making the low-touch PDR lane even more attractive for cosmetic damage. The trade remains fragmented among itinerant hail chasers and franchise networks of uneven standards. A disciplined, single-service brand with photographic guarantees and fixed per-dent pricing has the category's trust position open.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Dent Wizard (dentwizard.com) is the largest US PDR and reconditioning provider, serving dealers and consumers; Maaco (maaco.com) handles cosmetic paint and body repair through franchise shops; Caliber Collision (caliber.com) operates full-service collision centers nationally. Dent Wizard is diversified across reconditioning services, while Maaco and Caliber repaint and replace; DENT is the only one whose entire promise is leaving the factory paint alone.
Minimal.positioningStatement: One repair, done invisibly: the dent gone, the factory paint untouched.
Minimal.positioningRationale: In a trade where customers fear being upsold into bodyshop territory, absolute specialization is the trust signal — a company that cannot repaint cannot recommend repainting. The factory-paint preservation angle ties directly to resale value, converting a cosmetic fix into a financial one.

targetAudience.primary: Car owners who feel a genuine pang at the parking-lot discovery — leaseholders guarding turn-in condition, meticulous private owners, and used-EV buyers protecting factory finishes that cannot be color-matched cheaply. They are condition-sensitive rather than car-obsessed: the dent is a small wrongness they notice every single morning. Fleet and dealer reconditioning managers form the volume backbone behind them.

Corporate.brandDescription: Duty Cycle Group is a fleet electrification advisory that puts its conclusions in the contract: every engagement ends with a guaranteed total-cost-of-ownership parity date per vehicle class, backed by fee clawbacks if the math misses. The firm instruments client fleets for ninety days, models routes against real duty cycles rather than brochure ranges, and sequences electrification by economic readiness instead of optics. Duty Cycle Group tells fleet operators which trucks to electrify, which to wait on, and exactly when waiting stops being the cheap option — in writing.
Corporate.scope: Advisory and program management for fleets of 100-plus vehicles: duty-cycle instrumentation, TCO modeling, charging infrastructure sequencing, and procurement support through vehicle delivery. Sector focus on logistics, utilities, and municipal fleets. No charging hardware sales, no vehicle brokerage.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Duty cycle is the fleet engineer's fundamental measure — the real pattern of loads, routes, idle time, and energy demand that determines whether a vehicle can electrify economically. Naming the firm for the metric it lives by, in the plain Group form of engineering consultancies, tells fleet directors the analysis starts from their trucks, not from a thesis.
Corporate.industrySummary: Fleet electrification entered its post-incentive era in 2025-26: the US commercial clean vehicle credit expired in September 2025, California's Advanced Clean Fleets enforcement retreated, and the decision reverted to raw economics that now favor electrification on many but not all duty cycles. Utility interconnection queues stretching one to four years made charging-infrastructure sequencing the binding constraint, punishing fleets that ordered trucks before power. Meanwhile falling battery prices kept moving parity dates forward, class by class, faster than most operators' planning cycles. The advisory market is crowded with enthusiasm and thin on accountability — no major firm guarantees its parity math.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Inspiration Mobility (inspirationmobility.com) provides electrification-as-a-service including financing and infrastructure for commercial fleets; 7Gen (7gen.com) leases EV trucks and chargers with fleet decarbonization support; Voltera (voltera.com) develops and operates charging infrastructure for fleet customers. All three profit from electrification proceeding — they sell vehicles, leases, or infrastructure; Duty Cycle Group sells only the analysis and stakes fees on its accuracy, the segment's sole disinterested position.
Corporate.positioningStatement: The electrification advisor that guarantees its math — parity dates in the contract, fees at risk.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Every other party in fleet electrification earns more when clients electrify faster, which quietly corrupts advice. Corporate.brandDescription: Lane Five Remarketing runs de-fleet and resale programs for corporate and rental fleets, operated like an asset manager rather than an auction house. Corporate.brandNameRationale: At the great wholesale auto auctions, lanes are numbered and their reputations are trade folklore — running a car in the right lane, at the right hour, before the right buyers, measurably moves money. Corporate.industrySummary: Wholesale used-vehicle markets normalized through 2025-26 after the pandemic whipsaw, but with new volatility layered in: EV residuals swung on battery-health opacity and price cuts by manufacturers, while off-lease volumes recovered from their 2023-24 trough and digital channels kept taking share — ACV and online Manheim lanes now clear a substantial slice of commercial consignment. Fleets that timed disposals badly in the 2022-25 cycles left eight figures on the table, and treasury teams noticed. Remarketing decisions are migrating from operations to finance, which changes what the vendor must sound like. Nobody in the segment yet reports like the asset manager finance expects.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Manheim (manheim.com) operates the largest North American wholesale auction network with dealer and commercial services; ADESA (adesa.com) runs physical and digital wholesale auctions for commercial consignors; ACV Auctions (acvauctions.com) provides digital wholesale marketplace and inspection data. All three are venues that profit per transaction; Lane Five is venue-neutral, choosing among them for each vehicle and answering to a published index — the buy-side position in a sell-side industry.
Corporate.positioningStatement: The remarketing firm that manages fleet disposal like a portfolio — indexed, timed, and attributed.
Corporate.positioningRationale: As remarketing authority shifts to CFOs, the winning vendor speaks in benchmarks, attribution, and basis points rather than lane fees. Publishing a residual index creates the reference point clients measure everyone against — including Lane Five, which is precisely the confidence trick that only works if the performance is real.

Corporate.tagline: The rescue layer for the electric era.
Corporate.brandDescription: Mayday Response Group builds and operates EV-specific roadside assistance networks for insurers, automakers, and fleet operators — a white-label rescue layer with mobile DC charging trucks, EV-trained recovery crews, and tow-to-charge service-level agreements measured in minutes. Legacy roadside was engineered for fuel cans and jump boxes; Mayday Response Group re-equips the entire chain for stranded-charge events, high-voltage incident handling, and battery-safe transport. Client brands stay on the app; Mayday runs everything behind the button.
Corporate.scope: B2B contracts covering network design, mobile charging fleet operations, high-voltage responder training and certification, and incident data reporting across launch regions. White-label only. No consumer-facing membership product, no bodyshop services.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Mayday is the international distress call coined in 1923 at Croydon Airport from the French m'aidez — help me — chosen because it cut through radio noise in any language. A roadside brand built on the century-old vocabulary of professional rescue signals exactly what it sells: response as a discipline, not a perk.
Corporate.industrySummary: Roadside assistance hit its EV reckoning in 2025-26: electric vehicles approached one in ten US new sales and a rising share of the parc, converting the classic fuel-out call into the charge-out call while adding failure modes — bricked software, damaged packs, transport restrictions — that legacy tow networks are not trained or equipped for. AAA and major insurers piloted mobile charging with mixed coverage, and SparkCharge built portable DC delivery into a business. Motor clubs' contractor networks remain the weak link: EV-certified operators are scarce and standards are unwritten. Insurers and OEMs increasingly prefer to buy the capability as a managed white-label layer rather than build it.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: AAA (aaa.com) operates the largest US motor club with early mobile-EV-charging pilots; Agero (agero.com) provides white-label roadside programs to insurers and OEMs at national scale; SparkCharge (sparkcharge.io) delivers portable DC fast charging and mobile EV services. AAA is consumer-membership bound, Agero's network is legacy-tow first, and SparkCharge sells charging rather than full incident response — the EV-native white-label rescue network sits between them, unclaimed.
Corporate.positioningStatement: The white-label roadside network built for electric failure modes — staffed, equipped, and measured for the charge-out era.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Insurers and OEMs own the customer relationship but not the physical capability, and retrofitting legacy tow networks has proven slower than building EV-native ones. Specialization in the failure modes incumbents fumble — charge-outs, pack incidents, battery-safe transport — makes Mayday the low-risk contract choice precisely where risk is highest.

The emotional driver is exposure — each EV roadside failure is a brand incident for them, not for their subcontractor.

Corporate.brandDescription: Campaign Services Group completes vehicle safety recalls on behalf of automakers — and gets paid only per recall verifiably closed. The company runs mobile completion units, VIN-targeted outreach that reaches the third and fourth owners dealer mailings never find, and scheduling that meets vehicles at homes and workplaces. OEM service language calls a recall a campaign; Campaign Services Group takes the term literally, running each one with field organizers, completion targets, and weekly closure reporting until the population is done.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Inside OEM service operations, recalls are formally called service campaigns — the working term on every bulletin and dealer memo. Adopting the industry's own word, in the plain corporate Group form, signals a firm built natively for the job rather than a repair chain moonlighting at it.
Corporate.industrySummary: Recall completion remains the auto industry's chronic open wound into 2025-26: roughly one in five vehicles on US roads carries an open recall, completion rates for older vehicles languish below half, and NHTSA has sharpened pressure on manufacturers to prove outreach effectiveness rather than mail volume. Software fixed some campaigns over the air, but the stubborn remainder — hardware recalls on aging, thrice-sold vehicles — still requires physically finding cars whose owners no dealer knows. Mobile service economics matured enough to make driveway completion viable at scale. OEMs spend heavily per completion yet buy almost entirely on effort metrics; performance-based completion is the model waiting to be sold.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Recall Masters (recallmasters.com) supplies recall data, owner identification, and outreach services to dealers and OEMs; AutoAp (autoap.com) provides recall management software and monitoring for fleets and dealers; Sedgwick (sedgwick.com) manages product recall logistics and communications across industries including automotive. All three sell data, software, or process; none takes completion risk with mobile execution paid on closure — the performance position is empty.
Corporate.positioningStatement: The recall completion firm paid on closures, not efforts — campaigns run until the population is done.
Corporate.positioningRationale: OEMs face regulatory and reputational exposure measured in completion percentage, yet buy services priced on activity. Aligning revenue to verified closures converts vendor risk into client confidence and forces the operational inventiveness — mobile units, owner-finding, evening scheduling — that activity-priced vendors never need to develop.

They live between NHTSA quarterly reporting and dealer networks that treat recall work as unprofitable filler. Their careers advance on percentage points of completion; their nightmares are congressional hearings. They buy accountability instruments, not vendors.

The OEM asked what they wanted to run next, and the answer became the company.

Corporate.brandDescription: Yardmaster Vehicle Logistics moves finished vehicles from plants and ports to dealers with a railroad discipline the trucking-first industry never adopted: rail-first routing, marshalling yards run to timetable, and an unbroken chain-of-custody ledger for every VIN from factory gate to dealer lot. Damage claims, dwell times, and location are visible to shippers in real time, and every handoff is signed, timestamped, and photographed. Yardmaster Vehicle Logistics was built on a simple observation — the industry that makes the most tracked product on earth loses track of it the moment it ships.
Corporate.scope: Finished-vehicle logistics across North America: rail brokerage and management, marshalling yard operations, final-mile car haulage through vetted carrier partners, and the VIN custody platform. OEM, fleet, and remarketing volume. No used-vehicle retail transport, no household auto shipping.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: The yardmaster is the classic railroad job title — the person who runs a marshalling yard, sequences every car, and answers for everything standing on the tracks. Corporate.industrySummary: Finished-vehicle logistics stayed capacity-constrained through 2025-26: the specialized car-haul driver pool kept shrinking, autorack rail capacity tightened as OEMs rebalanced production across North American plants, and EV weight pushed loaded rigs against axle limits, cutting units per truck. Port and plant yards became the visible bottleneck, with vehicles dwelling weeks and damage disputes consuming margin on both sides. Shippers responded by demanding telemetry and custody documentation their legacy providers struggle to produce. Digital-forward entrants grew fast on visibility promises, but yard operations — the physical choke point — remain under-managed industry-wide.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: United Road (unitedroad.com) is one of North America's largest finished-vehicle trucking carriers; ACERTUS (acertusdelivers.com) offers tech-enabled vehicle logistics including transport, title, and storage; RPM (loadrpm.com) brokers finished-vehicle and freight moves with digital tracking. United Road is asset-heavy trucking, ACERTUS and RPM are broker-platforms; none combines rail-first routing with operated marshalling yards and per-VIN custody ledgers — the railroad discipline is Yardmaster's alone.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Finished-vehicle logistics run like a railroad — rail-first, yard-disciplined, with a custody ledger for every VIN.
Corporate.positioningRationale: The industry's costs concentrate where vehicles stand still and where custody blurs; both are yard problems, and yards are what everyone else treats as parking. Importing railroad operating culture — timetables, sequencing, one accountable yardmaster — attacks the actual bottleneck while the custody ledger converts damage disputes from litigation into lookup.

The buying trigger is a bad quarter: a port yard overflow, an unresolvable damage dispute, a launch delayed by transport.

Creative.tagline: Wear the edition. Peel when done.
Creative.brandDescription: The Dazzle Shop is a vehicle wrap studio that releases wraps the way record labels release albums: limited editions designed with commissioned artists, produced in numbered runs of fifty cars, retired forever when the run sells out. Your car becomes print 23 of 50 — photographed for the edition archive, wrapped for a year, then peeled and returned to stock paint like a gallery loan ending. The Dazzle Shop treats the automobile as the largest wearable surface a person owns, and treats permanence as the enemy of fun.
Creative.scope: Edition design and licensing with artists, certified installation through partner shops in launch cities, the edition archive and registry, and de-installation at term. Full color-change editions only. No commercial fleet graphics, no one-off custom designs.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Dazzle was the WWI camouflage program in which painters — many from the Vorticist art movement — covered ships in disorienting geometric schemes, history's greatest collaboration between fine art and vehicles. Reviving the word for artist-designed car wraps cites the exact lineage: serious artists, moving machines, temporary paint.
Creative.industrySummary: The vehicle wrap market kept compounding through 2025-26 as color-change culture went mainstream — driven by resale-value protection, lease-friendly reversibility, and social platforms where a distinctive car is content. Film technology matured with better cast vinyls and cleaner removal, while paint-protection and color-change segments converged in consumer perception. The trade, however, remains a service industry: shops sell installation hours, and design is a menu of stock finishes. Nobody has productized wraps as cultural releases with scarcity, authorship, and an aftermarket — the model streetwear proved a generation ago.
Creative.competitorLandscape: WrapStyle (wrapstyle.com) runs an international franchise of premium car wrap studios; Sticker City (stickercity.com) is a veteran Los Angeles wrap and PPF shop; Impressive Wrap (impressivewrap.com) operates Bay Area studios known for color-change work. All three sell installation services with customer-chosen designs; The Dazzle Shop sells authored, numbered editions — a label, not a shop, despite the name's wink.
Creative.positioningStatement: The wrap label: artist-designed editions of fifty, numbered, archived, and retired.
Creative.positioningRationale: Wrap buyers already pay for distinctiveness but receive anonymity — anyone can order the same film tomorrow. Edition scarcity converts the wrap from a service into a cultural object with provenance, unlocking artist audiences, resale storytelling, and press coverage no installation shop can generate.

They follow artists, not marques. The car they drive is often a lease or subscription, which makes a peelable identity not a compromise but the entire point.

Creative.tagline: Learn the car, then the road.
Creative.brandDescription: Mirror Signal is a driving school that teaches car control before parallel parking: new drivers spend their first hours on a closed skid pan learning what a car does at its limits — braking, sliding, recovering — before they ever face traffic. Built like a skate school rather than a cram course, Mirror Signal runs small crews, sessions instead of lessons, and a progression of named skills each driver signs off like tricks landed. Graduates leave with a licence and something the licence never tested: the reflexes for the day it goes wrong.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Mirror, signal, manoeuvre is the drilled mantra of British driving instruction — three words generations recite decades after their test. Taking the first two as a name plants the brand in the deepest folk memory the category owns, then subverts it: the mantra was about procedure, and this school is about what procedure never taught.
Creative.industrySummary: Driver education faced its reckoning through 2025-26: motor-vehicle crashes remain the leading killers of American teens, per-mile crash rates for the newest drivers run multiples of adult rates, and research kept confirming that standard licensing curricula barely touch hazard response — the skill deficit that actually kills. Meanwhile parent demand pushed advanced teen car-control programs like Street Survival and B.R.A.K.E.S. to capacity waitlists, proving willingness to pay beyond the licence minimum. The trade remains a cottage industry of aging franchises teaching to the test. A school that makes car control the curriculum, not the upsell, inverts the category's structure.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Tire Rack Street Survival (streetsurvival.org) runs weekend teen car-control clinics on closed courses nationwide; B.R.A.K.E.S. (putonthebrakes.org) offers free advanced driver training for teens founded by racer Doug Herbert; DriversEd.com (driversed.com) delivers state-approved online licensing courses at scale. The first two are supplementary single-weekend programs and the third is test-prep software; none is a full licensing school built on control-first progression — Mirror Signal's whole design.
Creative.positioningStatement: The driving school that teaches the crash you'll avoid before the test you'll pass.
Creative.positioningRationale: Parents buy driver's ed out of fear but are sold test-passing convenience — a mismatch the incumbent category cannot fix because its economics are built on minimum hours. Making limit-handling the foundation reframes the purchase around what parents actually fear, and the skate-school culture makes rigor something teens choose rather than endure.

targetAudience.primary: Parents of 15-to-18-year-olds — disproportionately engineers, medics, and motorsport-adjacent hobbyists who know what a panic stop feels like — purchasing on safety outcomes rather than price or speed to licence. The teens themselves are the second audience and the cultural one: kids raised on progression systems, clip-sharing, and skill trees who respond to earned rank, not lectures. The enrollment decision is the parent's; the evangelism is the teen's.

Creative.mission: To send new drivers into traffic already knowing what the car does when everything goes wrong.
Creative.vision: A generation whose first skid happens on our pan, not on a wet street.
Creative.manifesto: Mirror. Signal. Then what? The mantra always stopped one word short of the moment that matters — the moment the back steps out, the pedal goes long, the deer stands still. We start there. Skid pan first, traffic later. Skills with names, signed off like tricks landed, in crews small enough that everyone drives and nobody hides. The test takes forty minutes; the reflexes last fifty years. We teach the fifty years.

Creative.brandDescription: Featherweight Motors imports 25-year-old Japanese kei trucks and vans and does the unglamorous half of the job competitors skip: state-legal titling, insurance-ready documentation, a parts pipeline with stocked wear items, and an owner's manual translated into plain English and rewritten for the North American owner. Every truck leaves with a service history decoded, a maintenance calendar, and a named human to call. Featherweight Motors believes the kei truck deserves to be a vehicle you rely on, not a meme you gamble on.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Kei-jidōsha translates literally as light automobile — the smallest legal vehicle class in Japan — and featherweight is the boxing division where small fighters are respected as complete athletes. The name reframes tininess as a weight class, not a punchline.
Creative.industrySummary: The kei truck import wave crested into a genuine market through 2024-26 as the 25-year federal exemption rolled into the classes' late-90s golden years, with import volumes setting records and prices of clean examples doubling. The legal picture stayed chaotic — several states moved to restrict on-road registration while others, including Texas and Colorado, affirmed or expanded it — making title competence the market's scarcest commodity. Buyers shifted from novelty hunters to farms, contractors, and municipalities discovering a 10,000-dollar work vehicle. The import trade remains dominated by auction flippers who deliver a truck and vanish; the aftermarket — parts, manuals, service networks — is the unbuilt half of the industry.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Duncan Imports (duncanimports.com) is among the largest US importers of Japanese kei trucks and classics; Japanese Classics (japaneseclassicsllc.com) imports and titles JDM vehicles from Richmond, Virginia; Boeki USA (boekiusa.com) imports kei trucks and vans with dealer partnerships. All three compete on inventory selection and landing vehicles; none builds the ownership infrastructure — parts stock, rewritten manuals, registration advocacy — that Featherweight treats as the product.
Creative.positioningStatement: The kei importer that sells the ownership, not just the truck.
Creative.positioningRationale: As kei buyers shift from collectors to users, the binding fear is stranded ownership — a truck no shop understands, no manual explains, and one legislature could orphan. Owning the boring competencies converts a flipper's transaction into a durable brand, and positions Featherweight as the trade's adult in every registration fight.

targetAudience.primary: Small-holding farmers, contractors, brewery and campus facilities managers, and grinning pragmatists who realized a kei truck does 80 percent of a 60,000-dollar pickup's real work for a sixth of the price. They are competence-buyers with humor: the truck's charm sealed the deal, but the purchase was justified on payload math. Most have never imported anything and are quietly terrified of the paperwork — which is exactly the fear Featherweight monetizes by removing.

Creative.mission: To make owning a kei truck in North America as unremarkable as owning a lawn tractor — titled, insured, supplied, and understood.
Creative.vision: A million tiny trucks doing real work on this side of the Pacific, none of them orphaned.
Creative.story: The company started with a brewery: founder Dana Okafor imported one Suzuki Carry to shuttle kegs across a Portland lot, and spent four months untangling title paperwork that the seller had waved off as easy. By the time the truck was legal, three neighboring businesses wanted one — on the condition that Dana handled the paperwork. The fourth import came with a hand-translated maintenance booklet because the shop down the street refused to touch a vehicle with no manual; the booklet photocopied its way through the local kei community within a year. Featherweight was incorporated when Dana realized the truck was never the business — the booklet was.

Creative.tagline: Every part has a call number.
Creative.brandDescription: The Parts Library is a self-service salvage yard reorganized on library science: every donor vehicle is cataloged on arrival, every row has a call number, and the online catalog tells you — before you drive over — that a 2014 Golf alternator is in row 12, bay 3, with 41,000 miles on it. Borrowing cards replace haggling; pull fees are printed like lending rates; and a librarian in high-vis will walk you to the shelf. The Parts Library turns the junkyard treasure hunt into a lookup, without losing the treasure.
Creative.scope: Self-service yards with full digital cataloging, a searchable online inventory with row-level location, tool lending at the counter, and a core-return program. Passenger vehicles and light trucks. No mail-order dismantling at launch, no scrap-metal retail.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The name transplants the public library — civilization's oldest system for finding one specific thing among a million — onto the salvage yard, the civilian institution most famous for the opposite. Call numbers, card catalogs, and lending culture are real library technology, applied verbatim to fenders and alternators.
Creative.industrySummary: Used auto parts demand climbed through 2025-26 as the average US vehicle age pushed toward 13 years, repair costs and parts tariffs drove owners toward recycled components, and insurers totaled more repairable cars than ever on sensor-cost math. The u-pull segment consolidated around big operators while inventory findability stayed medieval: most yards list vehicles, not parts, and the customer's afternoon is the search engine. Digital pioneers like Row52 proved appetite for vehicle-level location data; interchange databases exist but rarely reach the fence line. The yard that catalogs to the part level and guarantees the walk-to-shelf moment owns a genuinely unclaimed experience.
Creative.competitorLandscape: LKQ Pick Your Part (lkqpickyourpart.com) operates the largest US self-service yard network with vehicle-level online search; Row52 (row52.com) aggregates u-pull inventory listings and VIN alerts across yards; Car-Part.com (car-part.com) indexes recycled parts from full-service dismantlers. Pick Your Part lists cars rather than parts, Row52 depends on member yards' data, and Car-Part serves the full-service trade — nobody catalogs a self-service yard to the shelf, which is the library's whole trick.
Creative.positioningStatement: The salvage yard where you look it up, walk to the row, and pull the part — cataloged like a library, priced like a junkyard.
Creative.positioningRationale: The u-pull customer's real cost is uncertainty — the drive, the search, the empty-handed exit — not the pull fee. Part-level cataloging removes the uncertainty while keeping self-service economics, and the library metaphor instantly communicates a system customers already know how to trust.

targetAudience.primary: Keep-it-running households, weekend wrenchers, independent mechanics, and first-car teenagers with more time than money — the whole congregation of people for whom a 90-dollar used alternator is the difference between driving and not. They span every demographic; what unites them is procedural confidence with tools and zero patience for wasted trips. A meaningful minority are restorers and hobbyists who treat the yard as an archive.

So we gave every donor car a record, every row a call number, and every part a place you can look up from your kitchen. Come with the part number; leave with the part. The treasure hunt is optional now — the treasure never was.

Creative.tagline: The sound the law requires, made worth hearing.
Creative.brandDescription: Motorik is a sound studio for electric vehicles — composing the pedestrian-alert sounds the law demands, the cabin chimes owners live with, and the acoustic identities automakers now ship instead of exhaust notes. Motorik works like a record label crossed with an engineering lab: composers and psychoacousticians on one floor, regulatory test rigs on the other, and every commission delivered as both a certified compliance package and a piece of music the brand can be proud of. Someone will design the sound of the next million quiet cars; Motorik thinks it should be someone who loves both halves of the job.
Creative.scope: AVAS composition and certification support, cabin UX sound systems, brand sound identity for vehicle marques, and a licensed catalog of pre-cleared alert suites for smaller manufacturers. No consumer aftermarket sound mods, no in-car audio hardware.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Motorik is the name music critics gave the propulsive 4/4 beat of 1970s German bands like Neu! and Kraftwerk — literally motor-like, the rhythm of the Autobahn rendered as art. It is the single word in culture where automotive motion and composed sound are already fused, which is this studio's entire business.
Creative.industrySummary: Vehicle sound became a regulated design discipline: UNECE R138 and US FMVSS 141 require acoustic alerts on quiet vehicles at low speeds, and with EVs approaching a fifth of global new-car sales in 2025, every manufacturer ships composed sound by law. The frontier moved from compliance to identity — BMW commissioned Hans Zimmer, Renault built sound teams, and brand-sound budgets migrated from marketing into vehicle engineering. Yet most OEMs still treat AVAS as a checkbox sourced from tier-one suppliers' preset menus, and smaller EV makers have nowhere to buy distinctive, pre-certified sound. The gap is a studio fluent in both dBA curves and taste.
Creative.competitorLandscape: HARMAN (harman.com) supplies automotive audio systems and sound management to OEMs globally; DSP Concepts (dspconcepts.com) provides the Audio Weaver platform powering AVAS and cabin sound in production vehicles; Bang & Olufsen Automotive (bang-olufsen.com) licenses premium branded audio to car marques. All three sell platforms or playback; none is an independent composition studio owning the creative-plus-certification bundle — Motorik's dual-floor model.
Creative.positioningStatement: The studio where the legally required sound of electric cars becomes the best branding surface a marque owns.
Creative.positioningRationale: Regulation created a mandatory creative medium — every quiet vehicle must sing — and mandatory media always professionalize toward specialists. By bundling composition with certification, Motorik sells risk removal to engineers and identity to brand teams in a single contract, a combination neither audio suppliers nor ad agencies can match.

targetAudience.primary: Two desks at every client: vehicle program engineers responsible for FMVSS/R138 sign-off who need certification without schedule risk, and brand or design directors who wince at preset chimes wearing their marque's badge. Concentrated among EV startups, Chinese marques entering Europe, and heritage brands electrifying icons whose engine note was the icon. The engineer approves the vendor; the brand director champions it.

Creative.mission: To compose the sounds electric vehicles must make until they are sounds people are glad to hear.
Creative.vision: A streetscape of quiet cars, each recognizable by ear, none of them beeping.
coreValues: The pedestrian is the first listener
Creative.story: Motorik began when an electroacoustic composer and a homologation engineer shared a bench at an OEM's proving ground, testing pedestrian alerts neither of them could stand. The composer said the presets sounded like appliances apologizing; the engineer said every good sound the composer proposed would fail the frequency-band requirements. They spent the winter building a tool that composed inside the regulation's constraints — treating the dBA bands like a key signature — and the first suite they submitted passed certification on the first attempt while a clinic of pedestrians described it as 'a nice car going by.' They named the studio in the van on the way home, when the composer's playlist reached Neu! and the engineer, tapping the wheel, asked what this beat was called.

messagingPillars.name: Composed inside the regulation
messagingPillars.description: The frequency bands and level curves of R138 and FMVSS 141 are treated as the key signature, not the obstacle. Compliance is designed in from the first note.

messagingPillars.name: One contract, both floors
messagingPillars.description: Composition, psychoacoustic validation, and certification support ship together. The engineer and the brand director sign the same document.

messagingPillars.name: Identity you can hear in a garage
messagingPillars.description: A marque's sound suite should be recognizable at ten paces with your eyes closed — the badge for the one sense badges ignore.

messagingPillars.name: The catalog for the rest
messagingPillars.description: Pre-cleared, licensable alert suites give smaller manufacturers a distinctive voice without a bespoke budget. Nobody has to ship the default beep.

dos: Write with studio-liner-note style and engineering accuracy
Name regulations precisely and translate them gracefully
Describe sound in plain sensory language, not audiophile jargon
Credit composers and engineers equally
donts: Mock the regulations that created the medium
Publish sound without the data behind it

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a Germanic geometric sans where the two O's are drawn as repeating waveform pulses of identical period — the motorik beat notated typographically. An animated version pulses at exactly 120 BPM, and the static mark always shows the pulse mid-cycle.
